estimates.basis: The older John Glasgow who held the Saltmarket Rankin–Young tenement in 1527 is assessed as the probable father of William Glasgow-1098. William occupies the matching parcel by 20 February 1528/29; the later St Andrew prebend rental retains its four-shilling burden, west-side street position and Rankin boundary. The 1534 family settlement and 1564 service as heir then directly identify the younger John Glasgow-1093 as William’s son. Read together, these describe a sustained family title rather than merely two men sharing a surname. Lineal succession from the earlier John to William is the preferred reconstruction, while the last William-to-John step is independently documented. The grade is now probable, below documented or strongly supported. This brings the formal local father assessment into line with the stronger property argument already developed in the research. The missing 1527–1529 conveyance has not been found. No inspected instrument calls William the earlier John’s son, and no recorded ages distinguish father from brother. A brother, collateral heir or purchase from a namesake remains possible. Indeed, the neighbouring Henryson parcel in the 1528/29 instrument passes between brothers; title succession alone cannot specify kinship. The combined parcel descriptions are correlated, and the later rental is not an independent record of the original transfer. Glasgow-1095 remains a provisional representation of the Saltmarket owner: its identification with the Stirling witness or the 1506 alias-Smith purchaser is not proved. The probable grade applies to the property-defined Saltmarket father hypothesis, not to every imported biographical claim. No mother is inferred: Eufame Craig may have been the earlier John’s widow, but this does not establish her as William’s mother. No Stirling parent, birth estimate, death location or identity merge is upgraded. The live WikiTree father flag remains uncertain; probable is a local research grade.

Select John Glasgow-1105 and Agnes Eastone-3 as the uncertain working parents of Thomas Glasgow-1226, the father with Catherine Clarkson/Classon at Uphall from 1717 and Livingston by 1730. Select Thomas Glasgow-1242 as the uncertain working father of Philip Glasco-146. Select Hugh Glasgow-3109, father with Jean Service at Irvine in 1696, as the very low-confidence working father of James Glasgow-4158, father with Margaret/Marion Rae at Irvine in 1721–1723. Select William Glasgow-1026 as the uncertain working father of John Glasgow-3481, the combined Calder father account recorded in 1730 and with Christian Meek in 1751–1755. Select John Glasgow-1057 and Agnes Spark-330 as the uncertain working parents of George Glasgow-4165, father with Margt at Irvine in 1741–1745. Glasgow-2462 is the proposed, very uncertain working father of the traditional Ulster ancestor Glasgow-591 and the Cavers Covenanter Glasgow-4138. John Glasgow-3375 is the selected very uncertain working father of John Glasgow-3018, treating the latter provisionally as the father named with Agnes Martine in the 1693 Irvine child entry. John Glasgow-1065 is selected as the uncertain working father of John Glasgow-2467, the John recorded with Mary Auld at Kilwinning for Andrew’s baptism on 26 October 1746 and James’s on 19 August 1750. James Glasgow-3526 is selected as the uncertain working father of John Glasgow-2847, husband of Margaret Anderson and father of the West Calder children recorded from 1745 to 1755. Patrick Glasgow-1440, represented by the Gordon Patrike baptism of 1667, is selected as a very uncertain working father of Patrick Glasgow-3920 of the Kilclone memorial. James Glasgow-1025 is selected as the very uncertain working father of James Glasgow-2988, the 1766 Corvanaghan householder, through preferred provisional identity with James Glasgow-1024 of Moneymore. Caleb Glasgow-363 is selected as the very uncertain working father of Lemuel Glasgow-2581. Neither Caleb birth is established by a birth record here, and Lemuel himself said he had no age record and only believed he was born in 1753. The younger estimate therefore lowers the second account’s preference without excluding it. No baptism, guardianship, deed or pension statement names Caleb as Lemuel’s father. A collateral connection to Caleb, another local Glasgow father or an unrelated Glasgow immigrant remains possible. This is a low-confidence named-family hypothesis, not a documented father clause.

Glasgow-2868 is selected as the very uncertain working father of Glasgow-395. The preferred model identifies Moores-284’s husband with the Robert Glasgow who acted jointly with Joshua Hartshorn over a Cecil County plantation in 1786, then places him in the local Glasgow-2868–Hartshorne-320 family. The joint Glasgow/Hartshorn association gives a more specific family-network clue than surname and county alone. The Harford family context and Cecil land occurrence concern neighboring Maryland counties. This is a conditional reconstruction, not a father statement in either notice.

The existing father relationship from Glasgow-3012 to Glasgow-3610 is now documented locally for the record-defined 1649 child. The supplied Scotland’s People index, Kirknewton and East Calder OPR 690/10/14, FR 15, names JOHNE GLASGOW as parent of the child JOHNE indexed on 22 April 1649. The preserved FamilySearch VQ4K-X6G account agrees on the child, father, parish and date. These are two presentations of the same underlying register, not independent records. Robert Glasgow-1156 is now assessed as the probable father of James Glasgow-1150, the Edinburgh weaver. Grant’s 16 June 1641 apprenticeship names James’s father Robert and places the entry at Wester Duddingston with William Crichtoun and master William Sclaitter. The 20 June 1649 burgess admission repeats Sclaitter’s name and the exact apprenticeship date, securely connecting the recorded son to the adult weaver. The Robert buried at Duddingston on 17 January 1647 fits the father’s name, parish and preceding generation, six years after the apprenticeship and before James’s independent household began in 1649. Taken together, the specific local father and the Duddingston burial favour one Robert over an otherwise unattested second contemporary Robert in that parish. The previous assessment treated the lack of a unique identifier as a reason to stop at plausible; the combined argument warrants probable, while remaining an inference. The apprenticeship proves James’s father was Robert; identifying that father with the burial account Glasgow-1156 is probable rather than documented. The burial index gives no age, son, wife or occupation, and burial in the parish does not itself prove residence at Wester Duddingston. A second local Robert remains possible. The two craft entries are a linked identity chain, not two independent statements naming the father. The exact scope of “servitor” in the printed apprenticeship wording need not decide the inference: the entry supplies the father’s name and Duddingston association. No mother is identified, so Deborah Ivey is not upgraded. Robert’s unsupported Archibald-1097 ancestry and his compatible identification with Andrew-3163’s recorded son Robert-4006 remain separate questions. Neither the later Fisherrow sasine identity nor the Edinburgh weaver’s possible Lindsaylands continuation is needed for this father conclusion.

Hugh Glasgow-548 and Margaret McCullough-1964 are assessed as the probable parents of Hugh Glasgow-540, the emigrant whose Pennsylvania will was made in 1827 and proved in 1831. William Melanchthon Glasgow’s family history, p.2, explicitly names the elder Hugh and Margaret as the married parents of John, Robert and their youngest son Hugh, born in County Londonderry in 1739. Page 3 follows this younger Hugh’s household through John, whom the author calls his grandfather, and its emigration in 1796. This is specific descendant testimony about a named family, rather than a parent invented from dates or a shared surname. The younger Hugh’s recorded will independently names the same four sons John, Hugh, Alexander and Robert, and daughter Nancy, within the corresponding Pennsylvania household. That agreement supports the family history’s identification of the emigrant and the reliability of its nearer family relationships. It does not independently name his parents. The explicit family account, consistent household identity and feasible generations together warrant probable parentage rather than leaving the father and mother ungraded. Parentage rests on one retrospective family account; later online copies and family trees are derivatives, not independent witnesses. Its author gives no Irish baptism or marriage source, and its 1824 death claim is contradicted by Hugh’s signed 1827 will and 1831 probate. The 1733 marriage, 1739 birth, older Hugh’s circa-1706 birth and Margaret’s imported vital estimates retain their separate evidence limits. The two adult Hugh Glasgow householders in Tamlaght O’Crilly in 1740 support an earlier local surname generation, but the return supplies no kin or townland. Entry 1272 remains a leading compatible identity for the elder Hugh; collector order beside Ellis and McCullough names is not proof of adjoining homes or of Margaret’s father. No particular 1740 householder or the 1772 subscriber is selected as this man. The 1827 will does not name the testator’s parents or his wife; it therefore cannot independently establish Margaret’s maternity or Sally Blair’s identity. No John-551 parentage, older William/Covenanter ancestry, Cameron origin story, or connection to Adam of Inishrush is upgraded. The two brothers retain their existing links and grades: John-549’s captured confident flags are not counted as new upgrades, and Robert-550’s separate life remains unverified.

The existing Moneymore father account, Glasgow-1024, is assessed as the probable father of Robert Glasgow-12 and, by inference through their established brotherhood, Arthur Glasgow-649 and Joseph Glasgow-1543. The catalogue description of David Faris’s 1990 genealogy explicitly identifies the Adams County emigrant Robert (1749–1839) as a son of a James resident at Moneymore. It identifies a particular father and son, rather than offering a same-name local candidate. The family letter of 6 November 1806 printed by Faris names Arthur and Robert as Joseph’s brothers; Joseph’s 1831 will independently identifies Arthur as his deceased brother and the younger Robert as Arthur’s son. These sources distinguish the two Roberts and establish the sibling group to which the father attribution can reasonably extend. Robert’s pension supports the County Derry setting and 1769 migration. The approximate generations are compatible; the circa-1722 birth estimate is not independent evidence. The positive father attribution and established family group together warrant probable parentage, while remaining below documented or certain. The father attribution survives here through a catalogue abstract of a retrospective genealogy; the book’s underlying parentage notes and a contemporary Irish parent record have not been inspected. The letter and will corroborate the sibling group, not the father’s name independently. Glasgow-1024 is used for its record-defined Moneymore father role: the inherited dates, Mary Harkness marriage, 1770 immigration, 1804 naturalisation, older James pedigree and proposed Corvanaghan identity are separate questions. The Corvanaghan identity and older father remain very uncertain. No probability is assigned to those claims by this review. The same father is inferred across the three established paternal-surname siblings; no evidence for different fathers has been identified. Other proposed siblings, including James-3305, John and Mary, and the proposed Adam connection are not upgraded.

Prefer the Glasgow child baptised on 19 June 1614 and the Archibaldus Glasgua who graduated M.A. in 1635 as the earlier identity of the Donegal cleric. The uncommon full name, compatible age at graduation, clerical career and 1639 Irish clerk occurrence form a coherent Scottish-to-Irish career. A baptism in 1614 places him at about 21 in 1635 and 25 in 1639. These are conditional ages, not separately recorded ages. No incompatible parentage or simultaneous Scottish household is identified for this proposed cleric. The other known same-generation Scottish Archibald, the Leith man Glasgow-3078, has a separately traced craft career: apprentice to cordiner Thomas Park in October 1639 and shoemaker/heir in May 1647. That positive career sequence makes him a weaker fit to the 1635 graduate and Irish clerk than the 1614 Glasgow child. It is a ranking argument, not an absolute exclusion or an assertion that a man could never change occupation. The Irish testator is securely the Ramelton/Rathmalton cleric by exact name, residence and profession. Assess his existing George Glasgow and Margaret Steuart parent links as probable, reflecting the probable Scottish childhood identification. The baptism explicitly names both parents, so maternity has its own record basis rather than being inferred from George’s spouse field. No Irish record reviewed names Archibald’s Scottish parents or university. The graduation and 1639 clerk entry do not themselves state the 1614 baptism date. Another Archibald remains possible. This is a preferred combined identity, not documented migration or proof that every early Scottish and Irish occurrence is one man. The quoted baptism witnesses are reused from the maintained reading, not newly checked against an image. Margaret’s own Stewart ancestry, George’s wider family, and the 1647–1661 ministry chronology retain their existing grades.

Betham gives the son no age, residence, spouse or estate. He could be another Thomas, so the Lifford identification remains inferred rather than documented. Select Thomas Glasgow-3556 of Lifford/Raphoe as the uncertain working father of James Glasgow-3001. The 1728 entry may carry an earlier deceased or dismissed officer’s balance, so it cannot select a generation precisely. The Tyrone James Glasgow-1025 and Belfast Captain James Glasgow-3172 are not merged with this collector or excluded solely by their unproved birth estimates and parent fields. No Scottish-to-Irish migration, exact age, mother, spouse or child of James is inferred. Thomas’s existing probable Archibald father and his other children keep their separate assessments.

Prefer the named George of Mureistoun as James Glasgow-991’s probable father. George is recorded at Mureistoun in the 1586 Calder obligation; the accepted 1605 original-register reading places James’s household in probable Muirestoun and names an adult George Glasgow as witness to the baptism of James’s son George. The earlier review already assessed the two adult George occurrences as probably one man. The same uncommon surname, the probable same holding across nineteen years, and the older name-bearer’s personal participation in the younger household favour lineal family continuity. Father is the preferred degree: an older established man followed by James’s child-bearing household is a normal two-generation sequence, and the child’s George name is compatible with that reconstruction. This is a combined locality/household inference, not three independent proofs or a compulsory naming rule. The 1605 witness’s residence and age are unstated, and Muirestoun remains a probable reading/location. Shared holding names do not prove a legal title transfer. Father, uncle, older brother, cousin and neighbour remain genuine alternatives. The 1586 obligation does not establish muster attendance, and neither record states that George was James’s father. The George name and witness role are supporting context, not direct kinship. Andrew Glasgow-3163 remains an unselected uncertain father alternative; his 1597/8 testament names Robert, Marion, Jonet and Isobel, not James. The George comparison supplies a closer holding-and-witness association than the broader Andrew/Calder model, without proving that Andrew could not be James’s father.

For the working tree only, select William Glasgow-3522 as George of Mureistoun’s uncertain father through the surviving possible identification with the Glasgow merchant George Glasgow-1099. Protocol 2903 explicitly names that merchant’s deceased father William; protocol 2916 gives his mother and curator. The same rare full name and compatible 1586 generation make the merchant an existing-profile comparison for the Mureistoun man. The father proof belongs to the merchant: transferring it to the Mureistoun account depends entirely on the unproved identity. This is a testable named upstream route, not direct evidence of a Calder-to-Glasgow movement or a newly proved son of William. The merchant was a minor in 1586, with the accepted approximate birth range 1565–1572. If James’s conventional circa-1575 birth were established, that would conflict with his being the merchant’s son. James’s birth is unrecorded: a later birth in the 1580s can fit the 1605 fatherhood and, toward the earlier end of George’s range, ordinary fatherhood in the previous generation. Those are compatibility examples, not new birth estimates. The 1598 marriage-contract comparison does not prove a first marriage or identify James’s mother. No date is altered to make this route fit. George-1099 stays a compatible candidate; there is no merge, no second distinct George son claimed for William, and no automatic transfer of Margaret Herbesoun or a wife as mother. If the two Georges are different men, William’s upstream placement must be reconsidered. The retained George Glascoe-36 and George-3171 comparisons remain open on their actual source limits.

Prefer John Glasgow-3193 of the Corsankell/Kilwinning family as Hugh Glasgow-1603’s uncertain working father. This materializes the leading Ayrshire placement already argued in the maintained five-generation map. The 1571 Corsinkell deed expressly names John as James elder’s son; the earlier Kilwinning tenant appearances are attributed to him as probable. Hugh’s surviving profile account describes an Ayrshire progenitor, his son’s account is centred on Kilwinning, and the following households lie in Kilwinning, Ayr and Kilbirnie. These successive local settings favour the documented nearby family over the existing Mid Calder/Inveresk father attachment, which depends on an online tree and has no movement, household or property bridge. A John-to-Hugh-to-John sequence is compatible supporting context, not a naming rule. Father is selected as a revisable one-generation model, rather than leaving the previously preferred local route only in prose. Hugh remains a tree-derived generation: no inspected contemporary record securely identifies him, names his father or establishes his own c.1600 birth. John’s before-1540 boundary means a birth for Hugh near 1600 would make him an older father, around 60 or more; a grandson or collateral position may fit better. Neither date is changed to fit. An earlier Hugh birth is possible but is not adopted as a new estimate, and no missing person is invented. The 1571 John is documented as a son, while his additional Kilwinning identity is only probable. John’s brother James Glasgow-3921, another local Glasgow family, an omitted generation and the former James Glasgow-991 placement remain alternatives. This is stronger locality reasoning, not a probable or proved father assessment. The 1677 deed-index Hugh, preacher of the gospel, remains an unresolved identity comparison and supplies no evidence for this father choice.

Select James Glasgow-1970 of the Cookstown Mitchell family as John Glasgow-2539 of Gortin’s uncertain working father, through the existing possible identification with John Glasgow-1968. The 1879 Hillsdale history specifically identifies James and his Mitchell wife as parents of John, a farmer near Cookstown. The Gortin account supplies another John in the same Derryloran/Cookstown locality and an earlier compatible father generation. The maintained Hillsdale research already lists Gortin John as a possible duplicate. This is a positive named-son comparison in the relevant family and locality, stronger than an arbitrary father chosen only from the surname. Prefer this existing family as a revisable home for the 17-profile Gortin branch; retain both John accounts separately. The identity is uncertain. The Hillsdale histories describe John and Jane’s seven children as Robert, Mary A., William, John, Bessie, James and Margaret; the Gortin account instead links Francis, Hugh, Letitia and Samuel. No child has been matched across those sets. An earlier union could explain different couple-based lists, but none is established here and no additional marriage is invented. If the seven-child account was intended as an exhaustive lifetime list for John, the extra Gortin group would conflict with it. The Gortin before-1771 birth boundary comes from Samuel’s reported 1792 birth; the Hillsdale c.1778 father estimate is younger. Literal 1778 fatherhood of a 1792 child would be about 14 and is a serious constraint. These are reconstructed ages and estimates, not two original birth entries; both are retained, without silently shifting either date. Sarah MacNeece’s status as the Gortin man’s widow and Jane’s identity also require testing; no mother is transferred to Gortin John and no wife is added or replaced. Another local John, a collateral relationship, or different father remain alternatives. The 1700s and 1800s family accounts do not independently prove these two Johns identical.

Select the older James Glasgow-1025 account as the Cookstown progenitor James Glasgow-1970’s uncertain working father, conditional on the existing Corvanaghan/Moneymore family model. The c.1700 and c.1730 estimates allow a father–son generation. James-1970 is already a surviving possible identity for the Cookstown-area Corvanaghan James-2988, whose selected working father is James-1025 through the separate Moneymore comparison. Extending that same unproved pedigree gives the Mitchell account a consistent, revisable place in the broader family. It cannot corroborate Drumearn residence, a death date, or this father choice. The older and younger James accounts may themselves be duplicates rather than separate generations; if established, the father edge must collapse. The existing older pedigree and the Corvanaghan/Moneymore identity remain unproved. The 1879 history reports Scotland-to-Cookstown migration about 1750, while the older James’s profile is placed in Tyrone; neither a return journey nor that Scottish birthplace is established here. Multiple James and William householders appear in the 1740 Derryloran return, and two James men appear at Drumearn in 1766. William or another local father, a collateral link and a separate Scottish origin remain alternatives. Mary Harkness is not transferred to the Mitchell account, and Margaret Rutherford is not assigned as its mother. James-1970, James-2988, James-1024 and the older James-1025 remain separate possible overlapping reconstructions, not independently proved sons or households.
